{{Short description|Jesuit Priest, scientist, and mathematician from the Spanish Netherlands}}
'''Odo van Maelcote''', (also known as '''Malcotius''')<ref>{{cite web|title=Van Maelcote, Odo|url=https://www.idref.fr/164062920|website=Idref.fr|publisher=ABESA|access-date=9 May 2018}}</ref>(b. [[Brussels]] 28 July 1572, d. [[Rome]] 14 May 1615) was a [[Jesuit]] priest, scientist and mathematician from the [[Spanish Netherlands]] (present day [[Belgium]]).<ref name="dbnl">{{cite web|last1=van Derek Aa|first1=A.J.|title=Odo Malcotius|url=http://www.dbnl.org/tekst/aa__001biog14_01/aa__001biog14_01_0234.php|website=Biographisch woordenboek der Nederlanden|publisher=DBNL|access-date=8 May 2018}}</ref>

== Biography ==
Odo van Maelcote, lord of [[Kessel, Belgium|Kessel]], was the oldest son of Johannes Van Maelcote, a doctor of both civil and canon law at the [[Old University of Leuven|University of Louvain]], First Counsellor and Vice-Chancellor in the [[Chancery (medieval office)|chancellery]] of [[Duchy of Brabant|Brabant]], and his wife, Marie de Viron. He entered the [[noviciate]] with the [[Jesuits]] at [[Tournai]] on 12 February 1590 and studied at the [[University of Douai]].

In 1607, he published in [[Brussels]] a small tract on the equinoctial [[astrolabe]] that he had designed and manufactured, which involved two conjoined hemispheres. The device was useful to missionary ventures around the world, as it could be used in both northern and southern latitudes.<ref>{{cite book|title=Visualizing Sensuous Suffering and Affective Pain in Early Modern Europe and the Spanish Americas|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=osZKDwAAQBAJ&pg=PA125|date=5 February 2018|publisher=BRILL|isbn=978-90-04-36068-6|pages=125–}}</ref> This made his name known among scientists, and when he sent an astrolabe as a gift to [[Christopher Clavius]] in Rome,<ref>{{citation|last1=Noyes|first1=Ruth|title=Printed gifts in Counter-Reformation Rome: Odo van Maelcote's astrolabium aequinoctiale. Early Modern Rome III Conference, University of California, Rome, 5–7 October 2017|publisher=Early Modern Rome}}</ref> Clavius responded by inviting him to [[Rome]] to teach mathematics and [[Hebrew]]<ref>{{cite book|title=Biografische Index van de Benelux / Index Biographique des Pays du Bénélux / Biographical Index of the Benelux Countries / Biographischer Index der Benelux-Länder|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=gQgiAAAAQBAJ&pg=PA904|date=24 July 2012|publisher=Walter de Gruyter|isbn=978-3-11-097714-1|pages=904–}}</ref> at the [[Roman College]] in 1608, where he soon became assistant to [[Christoph Grienberger]].

In 1610, [[Roberto Bellarmine|Cardinal Bellarmine]] asked four Jesuits, [[Christoph Grienberger|Grienberger]], [[Christopher Clavius|Clavius]], [[:it:Paolo Lembo]] and Maelcote, for their opinion on the new phenomena discovered by [[Galileo]] using his telescope. Reporting on behalf of his colleagues, Maelcote advised that they agreed with most of Galileo's findings, although they were uncertain whether Saturn consisted of three bodies as Galileo stated (the fact that Saturn had rings was not evident from the first telescopes); rather, it seemed to be elliptical in shape. Maelcote also reported that Clavius did not believe that the Moon had mountains and craters as appeared through the telescope; its surface was smooth, and the uneven distribution of some substance within the Moon merely created the illusion of an uneven surface.<ref name="Reeves1999">{{cite book|author=Eileen Reeves|title=Painting the Heavens: Art and Science in the Age of Galileo|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=QjlKMqlo26oC&pg=PA151|year=1999|publisher=Princeton University Press|isbn=0-691-00976-7|pages=151–}}</ref>

Galileo was invited to a banquet at the Roman College, on 18 May 1611, during which Maelcote pronounced a long formal [[eulogy]], praising Galileo's work.<ref name="Freedberg2003">{{cite book|author=David Freedberg|title=The Eye of the Lynx: Galileo, His Friends, and the Beginnings of Modern Natural History|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=6x5QypGKTS0C&pg=PA110|date=1 August 2003|publisher=University of Chicago Press|isbn=978-0-226-26153-9|pages=110}}</ref><ref name="PiccolinoWade2014">{{cite book|author1=Marco Piccolino|author2=Nicholas J. Wade|title=Galileo's Visions: Piercing the Spheres of the Heavens by Eye and Mind|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=VSYiAgAAQBAJ&pg=PA86|year=2014|publisher=OUP Oxford|isbn=978-0-19-955435-5|pages=86–}}</ref> Nevertheless, they were called to order by the Superior General of the Jesuits, [[Claudio Acquaviva]], and obliged to uphold the traditional [[Aristotelianism|Aristotelian]] view of the universe, which Galileo's discoveries overturned.

In 1611, Van Maelcote was back in Brussels, and from 1612 to 1614, he began a correspondence with [[Kepler]], particularly seeking his views on sunspots, following the publication of observations and commentary from both [[Christoph Scheiner]] and [[Galileo]]. Kepler agreed with Maelcote and Galileo that sunspots did not behave like satellites.<ref>{{cite book|last1=BURKE – GAFFNEY|first1=M.W.|title=Kepler and the Jesuits|date=1944|publisher=The Bruce Publishing Company|location=Milwaukee|page=76|url=https://archive.org/stream/KeplerTheJesuits/BurkeGaffney-KeplerTheJesuits_djvu.txt|access-date=9 May 2018}}</ref>

He returned to Rome, where he worked at the observatory of the Roman College until his death. Among his pupils was [[Orazio Grassi]].<ref>{{cite web|last1=Ribouillault|first1=Denis|title=Sundials on the Quirinal: Astronomyand the Early Modern Garden|url=https://www.academia.edu/26343382|website=Academia.edu|publisher=Academia.edu|access-date=9 May 2018}}</ref>
